analysis.one_liner: Suspends bee-killing neonicotinoid pesticides until they're proven safe for pollinators.
analysis.headline: The bill drew 47 House supporters but died without a vote, stalling in committee after referral to a subcommittee.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have ordered the EPA to suspend approval of the neonicotinoid class of insecticides — imidacloprid, clothianidin, thiamethoxam, dinotafuran and related chemicals — for seed coatings, soil application and foliar sprays on plants that attract bees, until the agency determined from peer-reviewed science and field studies that the pesticides would not harm pollinators. It would also have barred new approvals of those uses in the meantime and required the Interior Department to monitor native bee health and report to Congress annually. The bill cites research linking neonicotinoids to record honeybee losses, native pollinator declines, and harm to birds, and notes that the EPA itself found the seed coatings provide little yield benefit in most row-crop uses [S2] [S3].
analysis.who_benefits: Commercial beekeepers, whose hives have suffered annual losses as high as 45%, and farmers whose crops depend on pollination — the bill states pollination is worth $24 billion a year to the U.S. economy and that one-third of North American food production depends on bee pollination [S3]. Consumers benefit indirectly through a more secure food supply and lower pollination costs passed on to growers [S3].

how_it_helps.text: Suspends EPA registration of neonicotinoid insecticides on bee-attractive plants, trees and cereals until the agency determines, based on peer-reviewed evidence and a completed field study, that they will not cause unreasonable adverse effects on pollinators [S2] [S3].

Blocks any new conditional or standard registrations for those uses until that safety determination is made, closing a loophole the bill's findings describe as allowing prophylactic overuse of the chemicals [S3].
Directs the Interior Department to monitor the health and population status of native bees, identify causes of unusual bee mortality, and report to Congress annually [S2] [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Pesticide manufacturers lose a major product line, and farmers lose access to neonicotinoid-treated seeds and sprays on crops attractive to bees until the EPA clears them; growers would have to shift to other pest-control methods. The bill's findings argue the loss is smaller than it appears, citing EPA's own assessment that neonicotinoid soybean seed coatings provide little yield benefit and that 80–90% of row-crop uses are unnecessary [S3].

drawbacks.text: Farmers would immediately lose a widely used pest-control tool on bee-attractive crops before the science-based review was complete, and some crops rely heavily on those treatments for early-season protection [S2] [S3].

The suspension is effectively a presumption of harm — approval only returns after field studies the EPA itself must design — which critics in the pesticide and agricultural industries argued went beyond the normal risk-benefit standard of federal pesticide law (general knowledge of how FIFRA registration works).
Restricting one pesticide class can push growers toward substitute chemicals whose pollinator effects are not yet well studied.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The public benefit — protecting pollinators that support a $24-billion-a-year piece of the food economy — is broad, and the bill's own findings cite the EPA's conclusion that the most common uses add little to crop yields, which lowers the cost side. The real cost falls on a specific industry and on some growers who would need alternative pest controls. The main design weakness is speed: a blanket 180-day suspension, rather than a case-by-case phase-out, gives affected farmers little time to adjust.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the House Agriculture Committee and then to a subcommittee, and neither ever acted on it; it sat there until Congress adjourned, so it never got a floor vote.

narrative.text: Introduced by Rep. Earl Blumenauer on February 14, 2018, with 35 original cosponsors, and referred to the House Committee on Agriculture the same day [S1] [S3] [S5].
It attracted 46 cosponsors in total, all Democrats [S4].
On March 8, 2018, it was referred to the Subcommittee on Biotechnology, Horticulture, and Research, which took no action; the full committee never held a markup or reported the bill [S5].
No version of the bill was ever scheduled for a House floor vote during the 115th Congress [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Pesticide manufacturers keep selling neonicotinoid-treated seeds and sprays with no new restrictions, and no member had to cast a vote on them. Farmers keep current pest-control tools, but beekeepers and pollination-dependent growers continue to absorb pollinator losses.

sides.party_line_note: All 46 cosponsors were House Democrats and the bill went nowhere in the Republican-controlled House; no Republican sponsored or cosponsored it [S4].

industries.note: The bill would suspend registrations of the nitro-group neonicotinoids on bee-attractive crops, cutting off a major market for makers of imidacloprid, clothianidin, thiamethoxam and related products [S3]. Their financial interest in keeping sales running runs directly against the bill's pollinator-protection goal.
Beekeepers reported a 45.2% annual hive mortality rate in one government-backed survey, and restricting the pesticide class most strongly linked to those losses protects their livelihoods [S3].

industries.industry: Pollination-dependent growers (fruit, vegetable, nut and orchard crops)
industries.note: One-third of North American food production depends on bee pollination; healthier pollinator populations protect yields and lower pollination costs [S3].

They would lose access to neonicotinoid-treated seed and foliar uses on bee-attractive crops until cleared, but the bill's own findings cite EPA research that seed coatings add little to yields in 80–90% of row-crop uses, so many would face little real loss.
